oil.summary: Crude extended its blistering monthly rally — WTI up over 21% in a month and now at $91.55 — on a confluence of supply disruptions and geopolitical risk. Russian output has fallen to its lowest since 2009 as Ukrainian drone strikes force Moscow to process crude abroad, while the Deputy Prime Minister insisted the dip is temporary pending refinery restarts. In the Middle East, an Iranian attack on a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz killed two Saudi sailors, inflaming US-Iran tensions and adding a serious shipping-lane risk premium. Asian demand is absorbing available barrels aggressively: Chinese and Indian refiners are pushing Dubai crude toward $100 and paying record premiums for ESPO grades as Iranian supply tightens. Heating oil at $4.625/gal and US diesel near all-time highs reflect a global refining crunch analysts warn could persist into 2027. RBOB softened slightly on the week despite the crude surge.
drivers: Russian supply shock: Ukrainian strikes push output to lowest since 2009, forcing offshore processing and cutting oil revenues 22% YoY with Urals at $59
Middle East escalation: Iranian attack in Hormuz kills two sailors, lifting geopolitical risk premium across all crude benchmarks
Asian buying spree: Chinese and Indian refiners paying record premiums for ESPO and Middle Eastern grades, pushing Dubai crude toward $100

gas.summary: Natural gas markets are bifurcating sharply. Henry Hub slipped 1.79% on the day to $2.903/MMBtu and is essentially flat on the week, suggesting the US domestic market remains insulated for now despite the broader commodity shock. European TTF, by contrast, shed 3.37% today to €71.15/MWh but remains up 35.77% on the month — the one-day pullback looks corrective after an extreme run. The structural backdrop is bearish for European winter supply: storage sits at its lowest level in nearly two decades, setting up an intense LNG procurement battle between Europe and Asia. Asian spot LNG has already surged to nearly $26/MMBtu, its highest since 2022, on resumed Middle East conflict. Norway's seizure of a Russian cruise ship on behalf of Naftogaz adds further friction to Russia-Europe energy relations.
drivers: European storage at near two-decade lows, intensifying competition with Asia for winter LNG cargoes
Asian spot LNG near $26/MMBtu — highest since 2022 — driven by resumed Iran-related conflict disruptions
Henry Hub relatively contained on the week; US-European gas price divergence remains extreme

power.summary: The power and carbon space offers limited fresh price catalysts today, with EU EUA carbon ticking up just 0.25% to $79.195/EUA and broadly range-bound on the month (+3.09%). TTF, the key marginal cost input for European gas-fired generation, pulled back sharply (-3.37%) intraday though remains massively elevated month-on-month. The macro risk backdrop is deteriorating: the IMF flagged concern over surging global borrowing costs as an oil shock rattles bond markets, with UK gilt yields hitting levels last seen during the financial crisis. On the physical infrastructure side, Russia's Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant remains on diesel generators amid ongoing tensions, and Putin ordered fresh missile strikes on Ukraine's power grid — both developments underscoring acute vulnerability in European power supply heading into winter. Headline flow for this sector was thin today beyond war-related disruption themes.
drivers: Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant running on diesel generators; Russian missile strikes targeting Ukraine's power grid raise European supply security concerns
EU EUA carbon subdued despite macro stress — market awaiting clearer demand signal from winter energy trajectory
IMF warns on surging global borrowing costs as oil shock transmits into broader financial market volatility
